intro: Kasteel Helmond has stood here for nearly seven hundred years, and until the middle of the last century it sat in a large landscape park. Most of that went after 1921, when the last private owner sold up. Seven trees here still stand in what is left of the grounds, one a Chinese beech the register calls the oldest of its kind in the country. The rest of the page is a cemetery planted almost entirely in weeping trees, an oak beside a tower from about 1400, and an oak somebody wrote a book about.
meta_description: Thirteen remarkable trees in Helmond: seven in the castle grounds including a rare Chinese beech, a cemetery of weeping trees, and the Peeters oak.
question_meta: Helmond's oldest tree is the old oak of farmer Peeters at Brouwhuis, banded 1820 to 1830. Where it stands, and twelve more worth the walk.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Helmond is the one known as de oude eik van boer Peeters, the old oak of farmer Peeters, on the Rijnlaan at Brouwhuis, which the national register places in a planting band of 1820 to 1830, so around two centuries old. Its name is not folklore we have collected: the register itself says the name comes from the book 'Grote en kleine geschiedenissen rond bomen in Helmond en omgeving' by Maria van de Looverbosch, which is a local history of the trees of Helmond and its surroundings. That is worth knowing because it means somebody in this town went to the trouble of writing down what its trees are called, and the national register then read it.
question_context: Ages here come from the Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, which records a planting decade rather than a year, so every figure on this page is a band. The register is the 2024 edition and for most of these trees it is the only source, so everything is flagged. Seven of the thirteen stand in the grounds of Kasteel Helmond and share one piece of history: the castle has been here nearly seven hundred years, was surrounded by a large landscape park until the middle of the twentieth century, and lost most of that park after the last private owner sold it in 1921. The trees there run from the 1880s to the 1940s, so some of them belong to the private park and some were planted into grounds that had already become the town's. Two more stand in the Molenstraat cemetery, founded in 1880. Where a pin is marked approximate we know the grounds and not the trunk, which in a castle park is a real difference, and if you find one of these gone, tell us and it comes off the same day.

faq.q: What happened to the park around Kasteel Helmond?
faq.a: It was largely lost. The castle stood in a large landscape park until the middle of the twentieth century, and most of that disappeared after the last private owner sold the castle in 1921. Seven of the trees on this page stand in what is left of the grounds, planted between the 1880s and the 1940s.

faq.q: Which is the rarest tree in Helmond?
faq.a: The Chinese beech in the castle park, Fagus engleriana, which the register's own description calls the oldest and thickest of its kind in the Netherlands. The same entry's species field says European beech, most likely because the tree is grafted low onto ordinary beech rootstock. It is not the tree in those grounds that catches the eye, which the register also says.

We do not know, and that is part of the point. The oak carries his name because it was recorded that way in Maria van de Looverbosch's book on the trees of Helmond and its surroundings, and the national register took the name from there. The man is gone and the tree is still called after him.

faq.q: What is the Oude Toren at Stiphout?
faq.a: A church tower dating from about 1400, standing on its own. The oak beside it is a great deal younger, banded 1850 to 1860 by the register, so the tower had already been there for four and a half centuries when the tree went in.

All thirteen. The castle park is open ground in the centre of town, the Molenstraat cemetery is a general public cemetery open in daylight, the cedar on the Julianalaan stands on a public square, the Oude Toren at Stiphout is freely reachable, the wood at Horst is public, and the Peeters oak stands in public planting at Brouwhuis.

trees.name: The Silver Maple of the Castle Park
trees.age_estimate: roughly 125 to 135 years, from the register's planting band of 1890 to 1900
trees.story:
This tree is a fragment of something much larger that no longer exists.

Kasteel Helmond has been standing in the middle of this town for nearly seven hundred years, a moated brick castle that is now the town hall and museum. Until the middle of the twentieth century it sat inside a big landscape park, the kind that a private owner maintains and a town cannot. In 1921 the last private owner sold the castle, and most of the park went in the decades that followed, built over or reorganised into something smaller.

The silver maple, planted between 1890 and 1900, belongs to that vanished park. So do three other trees on this page. Together they are the best physical evidence of what used to be here.

Silver maple is North American and was planted for speed and for its leaf, which is cut into five narrow lobes and is bright silver-white on the underside, so the crown flashes pale whenever there is wind.

It does one more thing worth timing a visit for. It flowers in March, in small red and yellow tufts directly on the bare twigs, weeks before anything around it moves.
trees.access: Free. Open castle grounds in the centre of town.
trees.transport: In the centre of Helmond, at the Kasteelplein.
trees.how_to_recognise: Deeply cut leaves showing silver-white underneath, flickering pale in any breeze.

best_time.label: March, when it flowers on bare twigs before anything else

trees.name: The Old Oak of Farmer Peeters
trees.age_estimate: roughly 195 to 205 years, from the register's planting band of 1820 to 1830
trees.story:
Somebody wrote a book about the trees of this town, and because of it we know what this oak is called.

The national register does not usually explain its own names. Here it does: the tree is listed as de oude eik van boer Peeters, and the register says the name comes from 'Grote en kleine geschiedenissen rond bomen in Helmond en omgeving' by Maria van de Looverbosch, a collection of large and small histories of the trees in and around Helmond.

That chain is worth appreciating. A local writer went round asking about trees, wrote down what people called them, published it, and a national government survey later read the book and used the name. Farmer Peeters himself has vanished entirely.

The oak is banded 1820 to 1830, so it is about two centuries old and stands at Brouwhuis on the Rijnlaan, in what is now a housing district on what was farmland when it was planted.

That is the fate of most old farm oaks that survive: the fields go, the buildings arrive, and the tree ends up in a green strip with a street name around it and a farmer's name attached.
trees.access: Free. Public planting on the Rijnlaan.
trees.transport: About 4 km southeast of Helmond centre, at Brouwhuis.
trees.how_to_recognise: A big old oak standing clear in the green strip at Rijnlaan 125, far heavier than the street planting.

best_time.label: October, when the acorns come down

trees.name: The Oak at the Old Tower
trees.age_estimate: roughly 165 to 175 years, from the register's planting band of 1850 to 1860
trees.story:
The tower dates from about 1400 and the oak from about 1855, which is a gap of four and a half centuries between two things standing side by side.

The Oude Toren at Stiphout is a church tower without its church, which is a common enough sight in this country and always means the same thing: the nave was replaced or demolished and the tower, being solid and expensive to remove and usually owned separately, stayed. What is left is a tall brick object standing alone with a graveyard around it.

The oak came far later. It is banded 1850 to 1860 and at roughly 170 years it is at about a third of its likely span, which means that if it is left alone it will eventually catch up on the tower in a way nothing else here will.

That is the reason to come, and it is worth stating plainly rather than dressing up. Two hundred years from now a visitor will find a tower from 1400 and an oak from 1855, and the difference between them will look far smaller than it does today.

Go in winter, when the bare frame reads against the brick.
trees.access: Free. Open ground at the tower, reachable in daylight.
trees.transport: About 4 km northwest of Helmond centre, at Stiphout.
trees.how_to_recognise: The large oak standing beside the freestanding medieval tower.

best_time.label: January, when the bare frame reads against the brick

trees.name: The Beech of the Hunting Wood
trees.age_estimate: roughly 145 to 155 years, from the register's planting band of 1870 to 1880
trees.story:
The wood this beech stands in is a leftover piece of the hunting ground of the lords of Helmont, and the register knows what the farmhands used to eat in it.

The pool here is called the spekstreuvelvenneke and it has always been there. The name comes from what happened around it: farm workers took their midday meal at this spot, and what they ate was spekstruif, a bacon pancake. That is the level of detail a national tree register does not usually carry, and it survives because somebody local made sure it did.

The wood shows on a map of 1890. It is a relict, a fragment of a much older hunting landscape that the farming and building around it never quite absorbed.

The beech, banded 1870 to 1880, is a purple one, which in a fragment of old hunting wood is an incomer: somebody planted it deliberately in a place that had otherwise simply been left.

Go in October, when it turns copper, and find the pool. The pancake is not provided.
trees.access: Free. Public park wood at Horst.
trees.transport: About 3 km north of Helmond centre, at Horst.
trees.how_to_recognise: The purple-leaved beech in the small wood, near the pool.

best_time.label: October, when the purple turns copper

trees.name: The Oak of the Castle Park
trees.age_estimate: roughly 135 to 145 years, from the register's planting band of 1880 to 1890
trees.story:
The oldest of the four survivors in the castle grounds, and the one most likely to outlast the rest by centuries.

It was planted between 1880 and 1890, when Kasteel Helmond was still a private house sitting in a large landscape park, four decades before the sale that led to most of that park disappearing. A native oak in a nineteenth century park was not the fashionable choice; the fashion was for silver maples, copper beeches and conifers from other continents, all of which are also on this page. Oak was the sober option, planted by somebody thinking further ahead than their own lifetime.

That turned out to be the right call. Pedunculate oak routinely reaches four hundred years in this country. The silver maple beside it will be lucky to see two hundred.

A castle that has stood for nearly seven centuries with an oak that might manage half of that is a decent pairing, and it is the sort of arithmetic that only becomes visible when you know the numbers.

Acorns on long stalks in October, and a great many of them on a tree with this much room.
trees.access: Free. Open castle grounds in the centre of town.
trees.transport: In the centre of Helmond, at the Kasteelplein.
trees.how_to_recognise: The largest native oak in the castle grounds, with acorns on long stalks.

best_time.label: October, when the acorns come down across the grounds

trees.name: The Silver Lime of the Castle Park
trees.age_estimate: roughly 95 to 105 years, from the register's planting band of 1920 to 1930
trees.story:
This one was planted just after the castle changed hands, which makes it the last generation of the old park rather than a survivor of it.

The sale came in 1921 and the landscape park largely went in the decades after. A silver lime banded 1920 to 1930 is therefore standing on the hinge: planted around the moment the private estate ended and the public use began, into grounds that were about to stop being anybody's private garden.

Silver lime is the best of the limes to meet in person, for a reason you can see from across the grounds. Every leaf is covered underneath in a fine white felt, so in the slightest wind the crown turns over and flickers between deep green and pale silver. Nothing else this size does it.

It has a darker habit too. It flowers late, in July, and its nectar is hard on bumblebees, so under a big one in high summer you will sometimes find them on the ground. The reasons are argued over and the current reading is more about a starving late-season insect finding a huge low-value food source than about poison.

July, then, for the scent.
trees.access: Free. Open castle grounds in the centre of town.
trees.transport: In the centre of Helmond, at the Kasteelplein.
trees.how_to_recognise: The lime whose whole crown flashes white in a breeze.

best_time.label: July, when the scent fills the castle grounds

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of the Castle Park
trees.age_estimate: roughly 95 to 105 years, from the register's planting band of 1920 to 1930
trees.story:
A horse chestnut in a castle park is a tree planted for children, whether or not anyone admitted it at the time.

The conkers are the point. They ripen in September, the spiny green cases split on the ground, and what falls out is the glossiest object in northern European botany, a deep mahogany brown that fades within days of being picked up. Every generation discovers this independently at about the age of six.

This one is banded 1920 to 1930, so it went in just after the castle was sold in 1921 and the private landscape park began to break up. Planting a chestnut at that moment, in grounds that were becoming public, reads like somebody thinking about the town rather than about a garden.

The species is having a hard century. Bleeding canker has killed many mature trees since the 1990s, and the leaf miner moth, here since about 2002, browns the foliage of nearly every horse chestnut in the country from July onward.

So come in early May for the white candles, before the miner starts, or in September for the conkers. Not August.
trees.access: Free. Open castle grounds in the centre of town.
trees.transport: In the centre of Helmond, at the Kasteelplein.
trees.how_to_recognise: Large palmate leaves in fans of five to seven leaflets. In September, conkers on the ground beneath it.

best_time.label: September, when the conkers split out of their cases

trees.name: The Chinese Beech of the Castle Park
trees.age_estimate: roughly 95 to 105 years, from the register's planting band of 1920 to 1930
trees.access: Free. Open castle grounds in the centre of town.
trees.transport: In the centre of Helmond, at the Kasteelplein.
trees.story:
The national register lists this tree's species as European beech. The register's own description of it disagrees, at length.

What that description says is that this is a Chinese beech, Fagus engleriana, a species almost nobody plants here, and that as far as anyone knows it is the oldest and thickest one in the Netherlands. It also says the thing that makes it worth the detour: it does not stand out. In grounds holding a silver maple, a silver lime, two horse chestnuts and a century-old oak, the rare tree is the plain one.

The register files it under three headings that between them explain the confusion. Rare species in the region. Of national importance. Clearly visible to the public.

It is grafted, low to the ground, onto the rootstock of an ordinary European beech, which is presumably where the species field got its answer. A nurseryman quoted in the entry gives the reason for the graft: seed of this species will not germinate in this country, so a Chinese beech in Dutch soil has to be carried on Dutch roots.

The town's own records put the planting at 1930. The single independent record of its size gives 2.06 metres round and 16.4 metres tall. For a European beech that would be ordinary. For this species in this country it is, apparently, the record.

Nobody has checked that ranking. If you know of a bigger one, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the graft low on the trunk, where ordinary beech rootstock meets the Chinese beech growing out of it. It stands in the castle park and reads as a plain beech until you look at the base.

trees.name: The Holly of the Castle Park
trees.age_estimate: roughly 75 to 85 years, from the register's planting band of 1940 to 1950
trees.access: Free. Open castle grounds in the centre of town.
trees.transport: In the centre of Helmond, at the Kasteelplein.
trees.story:
This is the one tree in the castle park you will have to hunt for, and the register says so itself: it marks the holly as not visible from any path.

Holly is a strange thing to find on a monumental tree register at all. It is usually a shrub, it grows slowly, and at seventy-five to eighty-five years old this one is nowhere near the bulk of the maple, the lime or the two chestnuts around it. The register protected it anyway, and it wrote down a different reason for doing so. Every other tree in these grounds is listed as monumentaal. This one is listed as dendrologisch, a botanical specimen rather than a landmark.

What it does not say is which botanical quality earned the listing. Its history field for this entry is a single word: onbekend. Unknown.

The date is the other thing worth knowing. The band runs 1940 to 1950, which puts the planting somewhere across the war and the years directly after it. Nothing else on this page went in that late.

Holly is dioecious, so only a female plant carries the red berries everyone associates with it. Nobody has recorded which this is. If you get there in December and find berries, tell us and we will write it down.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the spiny evergreen leaves and the low dense crown, shrub-shaped where everything around it is a canopy tree. The register marks it as not visible from any path, so you will have to look off them.

trees.name: The Younger Horse Chestnut of the Castle Park
trees.age_estimate: roughly 85 to 95 years, from the register's planting band of 1930 to 1940
trees.access: Free. Open castle grounds in the centre of town.
trees.transport: In the centre of Helmond, at the Kasteelplein.
trees.story:
There are two horse chestnuts in these grounds, and on paper the only thing separating them is ten years.

This is the younger. The register bands it 1930 to 1940; the other, about fifty metres east, is banded 1920 to 1930. They carry separate entry numbers and separate coordinates, so this is two trees rather than one tree counted twice, which is a thing registers do often enough to be worth checking.

The decade matters more here than it usually would. Kasteel Helmond was sold by its last private owner in 1921 and the landscape park around it broke up over the years that followed. The older chestnut's band straddles that sale. This one's does not. Anything planted between 1930 and 1940 went into grounds that had already stopped being anybody's private garden.

The species is having a bad century in this country. Bleeding canker has been killing mature trees since the 1990s, and the leaf miner moth browns the foliage of nearly every horse chestnut in the Netherlands from July onward.

Which is why May is the month. The flowers stand upright over the whole crown in white candles, for two or three weeks, before anything has gone wrong with the leaves.

Only the register records this one. If you get there and it is gone, tell us and it comes off the page.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the westerly of the park's two horse chestnuts, the one standing about thirty-five metres from the silver maple. The other chestnut is roughly fifty metres further east.

best_time.label: May, when the white candles stand up over the whole crown

trees.name: The Variegated Cedar of the Julianalaan
trees.age_estimate: roughly 95 to 105 years, from the register's planting band of 1920 to 1930
trees.access: Free. Stands on a public square (plein).
trees.transport: About 0.7 km northwest of Helmond centre, in the Oranjebuurt.
trees.story:
In the Pacific Northwest this species reaches sixty metres and can live past a thousand years. This one stands on a square in a Helmond housing district, is about a century old, and is splashed with cream and gold.

The register calls it a bonte reuzenlevensboom, a variegated giant arborvitae, and then stops. Which variegated form it is, it does not say, and no other source names one. Several are in cultivation and telling them apart takes somebody standing underneath with a key. If you know which this is, tell us.

Variegation is not an advantage. Pale tissue carries less chlorophyll, so a variegated plant grows slower than its plain green parent and holds its place in a planting purely because somebody liked the look of it. Getting to a hundred years with that handicap, on a public square rather than in a sheltered garden, is the part worth respecting.

The register logs the setting as a plein, a square, and the owner as the municipality, so this was town planting from the start rather than a garden specimen that a street later grew around. It is banded 1920 to 1930, and the register's history field for it is blank.

Crush a spray of the foliage between your fingers when you get there. Thuja plicata smells of pineapple.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the foliage, flat sprays splashed cream and gold rather than plain green. It stands on the square at Julianalaan 45 and is the only variegated conifer there.

trees.name: The Weeping Beech of the Molenstraat Cemetery
trees.age_estimate: roughly 115 to 125 years, from the register's planting band of 1900 to 1910
trees.access: Free. General public cemetery (Algemene Begraafplaats Molenstraat, formerly Roman Catholic), open during daylight hours as is standard for Dutch municipal cemeteries.
trees.transport: About 1.1 km east of Helmond centre, on the Molenstraat.
trees.story:
Almost everything planted at this cemetery weeps. A dendrological survey of the ground lists, besides this beech, a weeping elm, weeping poplars, a weeping ash, a weeping acacia, a weeping lime and cypresses.

That is not an accident of taste. Nineteenth century burial grounds used pendulous forms deliberately, and a Dutch cemetery of the 1880s was working from the same nursery catalogues as everywhere else in Europe. Somebody ordered the mood along with the trees.

The cemetery was founded in 1880 as an expansion of an older Catholic burial ground on the Molenstraat, laid out with a central path and a Calvary mount, and it is a general public cemetery today. The beech is banded 1900 to 1910, so it arrived a generation after the ground was consecrated, into a plan that already had its shape. Nobody has dated it more precisely than that decade.

A weeping beech is one tree pretending to be a room. The branches arch out and then fall vertically to the ground, and a mature one encloses a space underneath that you can walk into. This one has had a century to build it.

The register marks it as not visible from the path, which in a cemetery full of weeping trees is a specific problem rather than a general one. Go by the leaf.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the beech leaf, oval and wavy-edged and glossy, on branches that fall straight to the ground in a curtain you can step inside. The cemetery's other weepers are elm, ash, lime, acacia and poplar.

best_time.label: late October, when the falling curtain turns copper

trees.name: The Silver Maple of the Molenstraat Cemetery
trees.age_estimate: roughly 135 to 145 years, from the register's planting band of 1880 to 1890
trees.access: Free. General public cemetery (Algemene Begraafplaats Molenstraat, formerly Roman Catholic), open during daylight hours as is standard for Dutch municipal cemeteries.
trees.transport: About 1.1 km east of Helmond centre, on the Molenstraat.
trees.story:
The register thinks this tree is as old as the ground it stands on, and it hedges the claim rather than making it. Its note reads: probably planted around 1880 at the opening of the cemetery.

That is a guess admitting it is a guess, which is worth more than a confident date. The Molenstraat cemetery was founded in 1880 as an expansion of an older Catholic burial ground, laid out with a central path and a Calvary mount, and the maple's planting band of 1880 to 1890 sits across that opening. A tree put in at a cemetery's founding has a job to do: it is there to be the thing that is already large when the first mourners arrive.

Silver maple is North American and grows fast, which is how it got into so many nineteenth century plantings on this side of the Atlantic. The bark breaks into long shaggy plates with age. The leaf is cut into five narrow lobes and is silver-white underneath, so the whole crown flickers pale whenever there is wind.

One thing to expect on arrival: the register logs this entry as two trees rather than one, so look for a pair.

The other silver maple on this page stands in the castle park across town, banded 1890 to 1900. This is the older of the two.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaf, cut into five narrow lobes and silver-white underneath so the crown flashes pale in wind, and by bark in long shaggy plates. The register logs this entry as two trees, so expect a pair.

best_time.label: late May, when the big winged seeds spin down
